People exchange their views in a conversation.
Pexels · 9811867
Making disagreement productive
Collaboration gains value from constructive disagreement, not merely smooth agreement. Two conditions make
dissent productive: a shared purpose that disciplines the discussion and relevant evidence that helps participants
revise their views.
A shared purpose gives disagreement a useful boundary. In a community exhibition project, debates about the
format initially reflected personal preferences. Once the team agreed that residents’ access mattered most, we could
distinguish essential requirements from choices open to negotiation.
Evidence then turns that common purpose into better decisions. Residents’ feedback revealed that the proposed
layout was difficult to navigate. This concrete finding allowed us to reconcile accessibility with creative ambitions,
replacing competing tastes with a problem we could solve together.
Constructive disagreement thus depends on both common aims and a willingness to respond to evidence.
Consensus is more valuable when it emerges from this inquiry. Good collaboration makes the reasoning behind
agreement visible rather than treating agreement itself as proof of success.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State two conditions for productive dissent. Develop shared purpose and evidence in separate
example-led paragraphs. Synthesise their contribution to sound agreement. Follow the main idea through two supported
points. The conclusion brings both points together without adding a new reason.
According to the essay, what makes disagreement productive?
